title: The Post-Observation Feedback: Why Timing and Co-Construction Make or Break It
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele addresses teachers facing early-term snapshot observations and learning walks, focusing on what happens at the feedback stage. He welcomes the move from top-down judgment to co-constructed feedback, in which observers ask about intent instead of asserting what the teacher should have done. He then names the main problem as unannounced feedback, which leaves the teacher recalling a ten-minute snapshot cold while the observer has prepared. His practical answer is an adapted Cornell method: write a chronological recall of the lesson on one side and the reasons behind each choice on the other, then review it before the conversation. He backs this with a short list of research on cognitive load, scripted reflection and psychological safety. The closing message is that preparing this way is a professional strategy that makes feedback fair, accurate and developmental, not a defensive move.
points: Co-constructed feedback replaces observer assertions with prompts about the teacher's intent, which makes the teacher explain their reasoning and limits flawed assumptions from a short snapshot.
Unannounced feedback is framed as an asymmetry, because the observer has organised notes while the teacher must recall details cold, and the teacher may reasonably ask to reschedule.
A Cornell-style recollection document, with a chronological timeline on one side and rationale and reflective tweaks on the other, turns the observation into usable evidence.
Teachers are encouraged to ask for two minutes to read their notes before responding, which grounds answers in what actually happened.
The post argues that structured preparation signals reflective capacity and that school leaders tend to welcome it.
quotes: In a co-constructed approach, feedback is a two-way, cognitively active dialogue driven by observer prompts rather than immediate assertions.
Instead of stating: “You should have done X instead of Y,” the observer asks: “What was your intent behind that activity, and how did it align with your goal?

Dropping feedback on a teacher unexpectedly creates a severe asymmetry: The obersved has reviewed notes, organised thoughts, and planned questions. You are caught off guard, struggling to recall a specific moment from days ago.
At its worst, feedback transforms from a developmental discussion into a courtroom cross-examination, with your teaching on trial.

You are fully entitled to reference your notes throughout the discussion. Taking 10 seconds to review your document before responding ensures your answers are grounded in what actually happened.
Trying to retrieve detailed memories from days prior while processing new evaluative statements overloads working memory capacity.
Using a structured recollection method isn’t about starting a debate or getting defensive. It is a professional strategy to ensure feedback is fair, accurate, and developmental.
